div.head: Timed and Resource-Oriented Statecharts for
div.p: Embedded Software

Jinhyun Kim, Inhye Kang, Jin-Young Choi, and Insup Lee, Fellow, IEEE Abstract-Embedded software should be correctly developed so that it is be compliant with not only functional requirements but also real-time and resource constraints. However, those constraints are often dependent on execution environments that are sometimes revealed in late development phases. In this paper, we propose Timed and Resource-oriented Statecharts (TRoS) to analyze the time and resource-constrained behavior of system in earlier development phases of embedded software development. TRoS extends Statecharts using timed action labeled with resources to represent actions that consume resources. This enables us to describe the competition among processes to use shared resources, and to analyze schedulability of embedded systems. We present a case study of a distance control module that controls train movement to keep the distance between trains for railway control systems.
Index Terms-Embedded software, formal methods, platformbased development, process algebra, statecharts.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: A S THE complexity of embedded software grows expo- nentially, a major issue in the development of embedded software is how to develop correct and reliable embedded software. Specification and verification methods, such as formal methods, along with traditional validation methods, have been recommended by various regulations and guides [1] to secure reliability.

Embedded software has a property of the reactive system in sense that it continuously responds to external inputs from the environment, and of the real-time system in the sense that its behavior depends on a timing constraint given by the environment. In particular, the real-time system is subject to both a timing constraint and a resource constraint [15], [26]. For embedded software, such a timing and resource-related constraint is often identified in a relatively late development phrase after the execution environment is determined, and one in which functionality is often reused under different time and resource constraints. Thus, MDA suggests a separate-concerns approach for the development of embedded software [4], but rarely pro-vides a formal approach for it, moreover the popularity of the multiprocessing environment complicates more and more the analysis of concurrent processes' behavior.

Statecharts is a popular behavioral description language for modeling a reactive system and embedded system. It has been recently supported by formal analysis tools such as model checking to prove the correctness of Statecharts models. In modeling embedded software using Statecharts, one of problems to be tackled is to preserve the analyzed behavior of Statecharts, in particular, parallel executions while being implemented. The behavior of Statecharts is based on synchrony hypothesis and pure parallelism [12], [19]. The assumptions obviously present great convenience in modeling the system, but unfortunately it is hard to implement such behaviors in reality, in particular, for software systems. Thus, in the case of implementing Statecharts using processes and an operating system, it is necessary to take into account time and resource limitation impacting on the behavior of Statecharts because the behavior of Statecharts in implementation consumes time and use resources, and consequently, the parallel executions may be serialized and sometimes even delayed. Therefore, it is necessary to complement additional functionalities such as scheduler for concurrent executions. Moreover, there needs to be a way to prove that the behavior of system in Statecharts conform to both the functionality of the system and timing constraints coming from its execution environment.

This paper addresses a model-based development of embedded software to mitigate that effort. In this approach the parallel behavior in Statecharts is transformed in the concurrent behavior of an extension of Statecharts, termed Timed and Resource-oriented Statecharts (TRoS), to analyze the time and resource-constrained behavior of the system bound to a specific platform. TRoS, we propose here, presents the notion of timed action adopted from ACSR [14], [15]. This specifies a timed and prioritized behavior in using a resource. One of advantages of ACSR for modeling a real-time system is that there is no need to model a scheduler for a resource because the resource using behaviors of are prioritized by the ACSR semantics. Moreover, the verification of ACSR is supported by Verification, Execution, and Rewrite System for ACSR (VERSA) [5], checks various timing properties of the system. Therefore, we exploit the advantages of ACSR in describing and analyzing the behavior of a system in Statecharts subject to a time and resource constraint.

Fig. 1 depicts our approach to the model-based development of the embedded software. The requirement for embedded software consists of functional requirements and nonfunctional re- quirements. Our concern among nonfunctional requirements is about the time and resource constraint coming from a platform. In our approach, the functionality of a system is modeled in a behavior by Statecharts, whereas a time and resource constraint is imposed upon an action of Statecharts [10] to represent a constrained execution of the action bound to a specific platform. Then, the model of Statecharts, along with the time and resource-concerned information, is composed and transformed into TRoS, to analyze a time and resource-constrained behavior of software bound to a specific platform. Some advantages of using Statecharts and TRoS in the development of embedded system are listed below: First, a platform-concerned behavior of Statecharts bound to a specific platform is captured in TRoS without constructing any additional behavioral models for components restricting the behavior of Statecharts. Second, TRoS is easily obtained from Statecharts by our annotation method using some syntactic sugar so that the model of Statecharts can be easily analyzed, targeted to a variety of different platforms. Third, the optimal resource and timing configuration to secure the correct behavior of the time and resource-constrained system is obtained through analyzing the system in TRoS.

We explain an application of our approach using a case study, where Distance Control Module (DCM), a part of a railway interlocking control system, is developed using our approach so that the safety of DCM satisfies IEC 61508 [1]. DCM is a digital control system responsible for controlling trains to keep a safe interval from each other. It targets to one subway station in Korea and is developed as a part of a prototype of a digital interlocking control system. The functionality of every DCM's function is first modeled in Statecharts and validated by the simulation of STATEMATE. Then, the timed and resource-constrained behavior of DCM bound to a platform is modeled in TRoS and verified by VERSA to prove various timing properties.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we discuss related works of modeling embedded systems using Statecharts. In Section III, the modeling aspects of TRoS are explained with a simple example. Then, in Section IV, the syntax and semantics of TRoS are formally given in a step execution algorithm. In Section V, we provide an annotation method to transform a functional model of Statecharts into a timed model of TRoS. In Section VI, we present a case study, where a part of a railway control system is developed and analyzed using our approach. Finally, we conclude this paper in Section VII.

div.head: II. RELATED WORKS
div.p: Statecharts is a popular behavior description language for various types of systems, such as real-time systems [6], [9], [23], [24], embedded systems [21], [22], object-oriented systems [7], [8], [11], [27], and even biological systems [13].

Harel in [12] analyzed the timed behavior of a system in Statecharts. Many other studies, such as [8], [9], [18], [23], etc., have proposed various ways to describe and analyze the timed behavior of a system. Harel complemented a special time event (timeout()) and a timely action (sched()) to give a timing constraint to a reaction of Statecharts. Similarly, the statechart diagram in UML also used the same time constructs, such as (when() and after()) [8], [7]. They all assumed that the behavior of the system is instantaneous and executes with the unlimited use of resources. Some studies, such as [9], adopted the constructs and semantics of timed automata [2] to define the meaning of the timed behavior of Statecharts. However, it remains challenging to describe and analyze the timed and resource-constrained behavior of the system.

Timed automata [2] and timed Petri net [20] also presented the semantics of timed behavior of a system in graphical notations, but there is no specific way to specify the resource-constrained behavior of system. Hence, it is complicated for them to capture a constrained behavior of parallel components subject to limited resources, because they need to model a scheduler for every shared resource. However, TRoS presents a notation to specify the prioritized behavior of shared resources using the notion of timed action, introduced by Lee in [14], based on Statecharts.

Algebra of Communicating Shared Resources (ACSR), a basis of TRoS, is a timed process algebra based on the synchronization model of CCS [16] that include features for representing synchronization, time, temporal scope, resource requirements, and priorities [14], [15]. The primitive actions of ACSR are divided into timed actions and instantaneous events. A timed action takes one time unit to execute and is represented as a list of resource and associated fixed priorities, e.g.,

. A distinguished timed action , or , stands for idling of one time unit. TRoS also provides the two types of primitive actions, timed actions and instantaneous events, to represent the timed behavior of Statecharts.

Ben-Abdallah proposed the graphical notation of ACSR, called Graphical Communicating Shared Resources (GCSR) [3] to analyze the resource constrained behavior of the system. GCSR is an automaton-based graphical notation for real-time systems and presents the hierarchy and orthogonality, just as Statecharts does. However, GCSR is not an extension of Statecharts, but an extension of ACSR, so its syntax and semantics are unfamiliar to the users of Statecharts.

Jang [25] and Park [17] adopted the notion of timed actions of ACSR into Statecharts. Their Statecharts specify timed action information upon a basic state of Statecharts, instead of specifying it in the time-consuming node used in GCSR. They can capture that the system consumes time and preemptive resources in a status using the specification. In this paper, we assume that any execution of actions needs to use and consume resources and time, thus an action of Statecharts is imposed by time and resource-related as well.

div.head: III. OVERVIEW OF TROS
div.p: The focus of TRoS is a timed behavior of embedded software that must be in accord with timing and resource constraints imposed upon it by the execution environment. TRoS is an extension of Statecharts as follows:

In TRoS, a system consists of a set of TRoSs that run in parallel and share limited resources. The prioritized use of a resource is represented by the notion of timed action, and communication between parallel TRoS is supported by instantaneous events. A timed action denotes a timed and prioritized behavior of use of a resource. It is assumed that an execution of a timed action takes one or more time units in respect of a global clock and consumes a set of resources during that time. Moreover, it is subject to resource availability. The notion of timed action is supported by a priority-based scheduling mechanism given in the semantics, based on the semantics of ACSR. Thus, competition for a resource is arbitrated according to priorities of competing timed actions. The availability of every resource is checked every time unit, and the available resource is assigned to only one process that requests to use them. The situation where two or more processes with the same priority access to the same resource is not permitted in TRoS. Unlike timed action, the execution of an event action is instantaneous and never consumes any resources.

Fig. 2 compares Statecharts and TRoS by giving an example of a gate control system. In Fig. 2(a), the gate control responds to two external events, TrainApproaching and TrainMovedOut. When a train approaches the gate, the controller perceives the approach by the event TrainApproaching and commands the gate to close by sending the event CloseGate. After the train leaves the gate zone, the event TrainApproaching informs the controller of that situation to close the gate, and the controller starts to close the gate by sending the event OpenGate

TRoS, in Fig. 2(b), captures the behavior of the gate controller from the view point of time and resource constraints. It also responds to the two events, TrainApproaching and TrainMovedOut by sending control events, CloseGate and OpenGate, except that it takes an action using resources and consuming time. It moves into the state GateClosing when receiving the event TrainApproaching. In the state, it tries to use two resources, cpu and gate, at the priority 1 for 20 time units. If it cannot use those resources, it must not exit the state and stays until it completes use of the resources. Similarly, when it receives the event TrainMovedOut, it also tries to use the same resources for 25 time units, and it can exit the state when it completes using them for the specific time.

In this example, Statecharts and TRoS have the same functionality to control the gate, but they are in different behaviors. The former executes actions instantaneously, but the latter requires executing timed actions prior to the execution of actions. In this way, actions to be executed on transitions are scheduled to be executed by time and resource constraints represented in timed actions.

A certain timed behavior of the system sometimes brings about a new functionality. Consider the TRoS in Fig. 2(b). The gate controller spends 25 time units to close the gate. However, even if another train's approach occurs during the gate opening, the controller must respond to that situation. Hence, the gate controller must be revised to respond to an approaching train while opening the gate. Such functionality comes from time and resource constraints.

Fig. 3(a) presents the revised gate controller in TRoS, where the state GO encloses two states, GateOpened and GateOpening, and its outgoing transition is linked to the state GateClosing. Using this correction, the controller is revised to respond to a train approaching, even when its opening the gate. to cross the railroad crossing if it is able to use it exclusively for 30 s; thus, it stands by to use the resource at the state TRCrossing. If it is granted the use of the resource, it proceeds to the resource-consuming state TRCrossing and uses the resources for 30 s. While the Train is crossing the railroad crossing and the gate is closed, the Car does not. If no train is over the railroad crossing and the gate is open, the Car can cross the railroad for 10 s.

In this way, TRoS helps the user reason a functional error due to time and resource constraints and take into account a functional behavior subject to time and resource constraints to analyze the system in terms of schedulability.

div.head: B. Semantics
div.p: definition of the semantics of TRoS is based on the step execution algorithm used in [8], [6], [12], [19]. The step execution algorithm: 1) takes the current configuration and input events as inputs; 2) computes transitions to be taken by selecting them from enabled transitions according to certain criteria; 3) make them be taken; and 4) produces a new configuration and new events as outputs.

Fig. 5 shows a timed behavior of TRoS. The timed behavior of TRoS consists of a sequence of macro-steps corresponding to the superstep of Statecharts [12], of each which consists of one or more micro-steps and one timed step. The micro-step of TRoS is an instantaneous step that consumes no time. A TRoS at a micro-step deals with all externally and internally occurred events, and the execution of micro steps continues until no event occurs. Meanwhile, a timed-step of TRoS is a time-consuming step. During execution of a timed-step, timed actions are performed for one time unit using either some resources or no resource. In short, TRoS first executes all input events and the events that occurred during executing input events, and then it executes timed actions for only one time unit, and it repeats to execute input events.

The behavior of a system in TRoS is defined as a set of possible of runs, each of which represents the responses of the system to a sequence of external stimuli generated by the environment [12]. The runs of the system start from the initial configuration consisting of a set of default nodes, and each subsequent system state is obtained by executing a step. A run is a series of detailed snapshots, called status. A status defined by the tuple , each of which respectively denotes basic configuration, timed configuration, current time, and input events.

div.head: V. TROS FROM STATECHARTS
div.p: In our approach, a timed and resource-constrained behavior model of Statecharts is modeled in TRoS. Statecharts is first annotated with time and resource-related information using syntactic sugar representing a timed action, and then the model is transformed into TRoS. TRoS presents functional behaviors and timed actions, and the timed action includes a scheduling mechanism to assign a resource to a process. For this reason, time and resource-related information is annotated to an execution element of Statecharts that may use a resource.

First, an action in Statecharts can be annotated with the syntactic sugar. This means that the execution of the action needs to use time and resources. Second, a basic node in Statecharts can be also annotated with the information, meaning that an execution at the basic node needs to use time and resources. Jang and Choi in [25] proposed an extension of Statecharts, where a basic node in Statecharts can execute a timed action. However, the execution of an action, including a series of operations in Statecharts, can consume time and resources. Therefore, we specify a timed action on actions of Statecharts rather than nodes of it.

Fig. 6 presents a model of Statecharts annotated with syntactic sugar representing timed action and its corresponding model of TRoS. The timed action is annotated on a transition labeled with , and the information is transformed with a timed action node in TRoS. This means that timed actions with the same behavior are serially executed for the amount of time units after the event occurs. In completing the timed actions, the action is carried out instantaneously. In this way, the syntactic sugar for timed action facilitates constructing TRoS from Statecharts, a functional behavior model, only by annotating timed actions. Fig. 7(a) and (b) present two models of producer and consumer, where there are two producers and one consumer as parallel components, and two resources, cpu and the buffer of the size , denoted by buff, shared by those components. The producers are initiated by external events, cmd1 and cmd2 to pro- duce data, and the consumer executes a data processing if any data exist in the buffer. Provided the producers and the consumer are initiated at the same time, the operation write(buff) of two producers and the operation read (buff) are simultaneously executed to access buff, and consequently the results of their accesses to the data are undetermined. That is, there needs to be a solution to mediate their access the data. Fig. 7(b) shows prioritized concurrent behaviors of the components of Fig. 7(a) given by time and resource-related information in the form of timed action. The parallel components are in competition for shared resources, cpu and buff, with their own priorities. If their execution conditions hold, they want to preempt those resources to execute according to priorities. If the three competitors are simultaneously initiated, PRODUCER1 first accesses the data buff, then PRODUCER1 does it. CONSUMER accesses it only when neither of the two components is accessing the data. In this way, the prioritized concurrent behaviors of the components are specified with only time and resource related information, not constructing any schedulers for the resources.

It is possible for a constraint annotated on the behavior of Statecharts to cause an error. The error occurs while applying the constraint concerning time and resources to the behavior of Statecharts. Thus, the error must be fixed through elaborating assignment of resources to executions of parallel behaviors of Statecharts consuming the resources or by scheduling the parallel executions of Statecharts to conform to functional and timing requirements.

div.head: VI. CASE STUDY: DISTANCE CONTROL MODULE IN RAILWAY CONTROL SYSTEM
div.p: To explain how to use TRoS in the development of embedded system, we present here a case study, where our approach is applied to the development of a part of an interlocking system in the railway control system, called Distance Control Module (DCM). DCM is a digital control system used in subway stations in Korea. It is responsible for controlling trains to maintain a safe distance between one another. To control the train's movement, DCM uses a control message, PMA (Permissive Movement Authority), that implies information about status of the block the trains run on; first, All trains within DCM control area send to DCM a message about their current status such as position, speed, and direction. Second, DCM updates PMA based on the information plus commands from its environments such as Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) and Control Route Distance (CRD). Third, it sends the corresponding PMA to every train within its control area. Finally, the trains make a decision for their movement, referring to PMA from DCM. The DCM's procedure to control trains repeats continuously.

The development of DCM is divided into three phrases: First, the conceptual requirement of DCM is specified in a natural language and validated by user and engineer's review. Second, the functional requirement of DCM in natural language is modeled using Statecharts. The models of DCM are validated by a simulation tool supported by STATEMATE. Third, the TRoS of DCM, timing and resource constrained models, are constructed by annotating timed actions directly upon the Statecharts of DCM. The TRoS of DCM is verified in respect of schedulability by translating TRoS into ACSR whose behavior is equivalent to the timed behavior of TRoS and by checking the ACSR model of DCM with VERSA. based on the information it has collected from various sources, such as trains, the interlocking system, ATP, and ATS. These main functionalities are designed by seven functions described in Activity-charts, shown in Fig. 8, where the functionality of each function is modeled in Statecharts. The chart "@DCM_ACTIVITY" is a Control Activity chart that initiates the execution of components.

div.head: A. DCM in Statecharts
div.p: The validation of the models in Statecharts is performed by the simulation of STATEMATE, where we checked if the modeled system in Statecharts conforms to scenarios that describe the expected behaviors of DCM. Using the simulation for DCM In this requirement, a train must stop whenever the value of PMA for a block where the train runs on is set to RED. This requirement causes a deadlock situation, where two trains crossing at an intersection prevent each from further movement.

Fig. 9 shows a deadlock situation among DCM's behaviors, where DCM sets to RED the value of PMA for the immediate rear block of a block occupied by two trains, 1 and 2, without any other consideration, and consequently they block each other. This defect is rooted in the incompleteness of functional requirements of DCM, and we could fix it through detailing the functionality of setting the value of PMA.

div.head: B. DCM in TRoS
div.p: The timed and resource-constrained behaviors of DCM are captured in TRoS that is extended from Statecharts by means of the annotation method we present here. Time and resourcerelated information is annotated on the model of DCM, based on the timing and resource constraints in Table I, which lists the information about priority, the worst execution time, and necessary resources of each function in DCM. I, and allows capturing timed and resource-constrained behavior of each function. The DCM functions in TRoS are regarded as concurrent processes. If a condition to initiate an execution of a process is satisfied, the process starts to execute, interacting with other processes. The execution of a process is dependent on the availability of resources. The two models of TRoS in Fig. 10 are in competition to use the resource and , and they cannot execute if any resources are not secured. In the same way, the timed and prioritized behavior of a system supported by a multiprocessor environment can be also easily captured in TRoS.

To formally analyze the TRoS of DCM by VERSA, the TRoS of DCM needs to be translated into a model of ACSR. In this paper, we do not specify how to translate TRoS into ACSR. Table II shows the ACSR of DCM's two functions, MANAGE-MENT_BLC_STAT and BLC_OPEN_CLOSE, translated from the TRos of DCM. VERSA checked if the behaviors of DCM's functions result in any collision in preempting any shared resources and miss the deadline of each function. The result of the verification is shown in Fig. 11, saying that "true(by prioritized strong equivalence)," which means that there is no resource collision and no deadline miss during executing DCM's functions in ACSR for the given resource configuration, scheduling policies, and timing constraints for DCM's functions.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: The more popular the multiprocessing environment for application software becomes, the more important the correctness of application software bound to the execution environment becomes. In the development of embedded software using Statecharts, however, it is not easy to describe the behavior of software bound to an execution environment using only Statecharts. In particular, in the case where parallel behaviors of Statecharts is implemented into concurrent behaviors of processes, it is important to preserve the analyzed properties of models at implementation. This paper presented an extension of Statecharts, called TRoS, that provides the notion of timed action as well as all the descriptive elements of Statecharts. A timed action represents a behavior of timed and prioritized use of a resource, so the processes in timed actions are in competition and chosen to execute by a scheduler given in semantics. Therefore, the behaviors of the system prioritized to a resource can be easily captured by TRoS, without modeling additional scheduling models. Moreover, the extensibility of Statecharts to TRoS, using our annotation method makes a verifiable and platform-concerned behavior for existing models of Statecharts be more attainable.

In this sense, TRoS is suited to the development of embedded software along with Statecharts. There are two reasons: First, it presents a timed behavior model of systems subject to resource availability, as well as reaction time. Second, the existing model of Statecharts is transformed into its corresponding model in TRoS, which includes a platform-concerned behavior of system as well. The case study we presented here showed how to apply our approach to the development of embedded systems. In the case study, the functional model for a digital control software for a railway control system, DCM, was first developed using Statecharts. Then, its timed and resource-constrained model was reconstructed in TRoS. Using our analysis for Statecharts and TRoS, the functional behavior of DCM is shown to be correct for given functional properties, and the timed and resource-constrained behavior is shown to be correct for given timing and resource constraints.

DCM consists of five main control functions; block open and close control, temporary speed control, train direction monitor, train location verification, and train distance control. • Block open and close control: deals with the command concerning block open and close from ATP. It delivers the result of processing the command to the relevant trains via PMA. • Temporary speed control: deals with the command concerning setting temporary speed on a specific block. The command is also delivered to the relevant trains via PMA. • Train direction monitor: monitors the direction of trains to check if they move to the correct direction. • Train location (position) verification: verifies the position of trains and updates the relevant status of blocks. • Train distance control: controls the movement of trains
